newsitem.title: RUSSIA: Yeltsin, Chernomyrdin discuss govt shake-up, army.
newsitem.headline: Yeltsin, Chernomyrdin discuss govt shake-up, army.

text.p: President Boris Yeltsin and Prime Minister Viktor Chernomyrdin met on Thursday to put the final touches to a radical government shake-up aimed at slashing bureaucracy and reviving Russia's flagging market reforms.

Kremlin press secretary Sergei Yastrzhembsky said the two men discussed the new cabinet structure and personnel issues and also the thorny question of financing for Russia's demoralised, cash-strapped armed forces.
But it was not clear whether the meeting, coming after a week of high suspense and uncertainty in Russian politics, would bring any immediate announcement on the new government line-up.

"It is possible to assume that by the time the president leaves for Helsinki (for his summit meeting with U.S. President Bill Clinton on March 19) there will be maximum clarity in this matter," Yastrzhembsky told Ekho Moskvy radio in an interview.

Dozens of ministers have been on tentershooks waiting to hear of their fate since Yeltsin, blasting the government for failing to tackle Russia's economic and social ills, ordered Chernomyrdin to reshuffle his team.
Yeltsin, newly back at the helm after many months of illness, has made clear only Chernomyrdin and newly appointed First Deputy Prime Minister Anatoly Chubais are assured of keeping their jobs.

Chubais, a liberal, will be the sole first deputy premier in the new line-up -- there are four now -- and the number of ministers will also be cut, helping to reduce a bloated government bureaucracy little changed from Soviet times.
Chernomyrdin said on Wednesday his new cabinet, which he has promised to present by the end of the week, would be younger and more professional and include market-minded reformers.
He added that most new ministers would be under 50 and have administrative experience.
After his talks with Yeltsin, Chernomyrdin chaired a meeting of the Defence Council, which was expected to discuss Russia's position on NATO's expansion plans.

The Atlantic alliance's intention to invite in several former Warsaw Pact members later this year has stirred fierce opposition in Moscow, which sees NATO expansion as a threat to its own security. The issue is set to dominate Yeltsin's summit meeting with Clinton next week.
"The (Helsinki) talks will be very concrete, rather firm and even tough because the protection of Russia's vital interests is at stake," said Yastrzhembsky in his radio interview.
Yastrzhembsky said the two presidents would also discuss U.S.-Russian economic relations, including Moscow's efforts to win better access for its exports in American and world markets.

Yeltsin's anxiety over Russia's economic plight -- stagnant output, a big backlog in wages and pensions, low tax revenues -- sparked his decision to draft Chubais back into the government with broad responsibility for reforms, Yastrzhembsky said.
"The appearance of Anatoly Borisovich (Chubais) in government will strengthen the cabinet," he added.
Architect of Russia's tough privatisation drive in 1992-1996, Chubais is a hate figure for the communist opposition who accuse him of selling off Russian state firms too cheaply.
They also cannot forgive the youthful reformer for helping to spearhead Yeltsin's re-election campaign last summer. Until now Chubais had been in charge of the Kremlin administration.

In a non-binding resolution approved on Wednesday, the communist-dominated State Duma lower house of parliament condemned Chubais' nomination as "a provocation to public opinion" and said the reshuffle would lead Russia to ruin.
Returning to the attack on Thursday, the Duma's communist speaker Gennady Seleznyov urged Yeltsin to reconsider.
"The president must understand that if Chubais' team comes to power the crisis will deepen. They have a pro-Western orientation," he said.
